desc:
Given an array nums of non-negative integers, count the subsets that contain exactly k elements and whose elements add up to exactly target. A subset is chosen by index, so equal values at different positions give different subsets.

The count can be large; return it modulo 1,000,000,007.

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 2, target = 6 -> 2    ({1,5} and {2,4})
nums = [2, 2, 2, 2],    k = 2, target = 4 -> 6    (any two of the four 2s)
nums = [0, 0, 3],       k = 2, target = 3 -> 2    ({0,3} using either zero)
hints: Counting subsets with a given sum is a standard DP. Now there is a second condition: the number of chosen elements.
Let ways[j][s] be the number of subsets with exactly j elements and sum s, among the elements seen so far. ways[0][0] = 1.
For each element x, update ways[j][s] += ways[j-1][s-x] with j going from k down to 1 so that the element is used once. Reduce modulo 1,000,000,007. The answer is ways[k][target].
editorial: Extend the counting knapsack by one more axis. ways[j][s] counts the subsets of the processed elements that have exactly j elements and sum exactly s. The empty subset gives ways[0][0] = 1. When an element x is added, every subset counted in ways[j-1][s-x] can be extended by x to a subset counted in ways[j][s], so ways[j][s] grows by that amount.

To use each element once, the rows are updated from j = k down to 1, so the row j - 1 being read still reflects the situation before the current element. Elements equal to 0 are handled correctly: they extend a subset without changing the sum, and each zero is a different index. The count is taken modulo 1,000,000,007. Time O(n · k · target), space O(k · target).
